claims.text: The baseline is a single-phase FCC magnetic high-entropy alloy, such as a CrCoNi-based alloy.
The baseline alloy has relatively low coercivity.
Adding approximately 1–1.5 wt% Pd will increase the coercive field.
Fine-tuning the Co concentration will increase the coercive field.
Fine-tuning Co concentration is equivalent to adding a minor amount of Pd for purposes of increasing coercivity.
Pd addition or Co optimization increases the lattice parameter.
Pd addition or Co optimization creates local compositional inhomogeneities.
Pd addition or Co optimization enhances local magnetic anisotropy by altering the local electronic and crystallographic environment.
The intervention forms additional domain-wall pinning centers.
Increased local magnetic anisotropy promotes stronger domain-wall pinning.
Stronger pinning hinders domain-wall motion and thereby increases coercivity.
The modified alloy will have a noticeably higher coercive field than a compositionally and processing-matched baseline.
Prior evidence suggests a significant enhancement in coercivity after the intervention.
Pd incorporation can homogenize magnetic properties.
Prior evidence supports improved exchange behavior in the modified alloy.
The coercivity increase should hold in chemically homogeneous, single-phase FCC alloys whose coercivity is governed primarily by domain-wall motion.
The intervention may not have the same effect in non-FCC or multiphase alloys, or when processing variables dominate pinning behavior.
The effect is expected under controlled, potentially cryogenic SQUID or VSM measurement conditions after matched rolling and annealing.
Matched intervention and control samples should be processed identically and compared by magnetic hysteresis measurements.
Failure to observe a statistically significant coercivity increase, or failure to observe enhanced pinning-center density, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The required starting state is described as highly chemically homogeneous and the predicted state as more magnetically homogeneous, while the proposed mediator is the creation of local compositional inhomogeneities. The hypothesis does not distinguish macroscopic homogeneity from local fluctuations sufficiently to resolve this tension.

The requested single intervention is presented as two alternatives—Pd addition or Co-concentration adjustment—and they are treated as equivalent despite having different compositions, controls, and no cited evidence establishing equivalence.
